"""A requirement that changes after the agents worked with it is said out loud, on invented values (no scenario
values): the agents are told, the open question keeps saying it, and an "absent" given for the old values is void."""
import json
import sys
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

import casefile  # noqa: E402
import worker  # noqa: E402

AMENDMENT = {"answers": [{"number": "Q-1", "timestamp": "2029-12-20T10:00:00Z", "tech_amendments": [
    {"revision": "B", "requirement_ref": "REQ-1", "attribute": "stroke", "value": "200"}]}]}


def case(stroke: int = 207, **requirement) -> casefile.CaseFile:
    """A tender with one position whose requirement is on file in the current revision."""
    facts = casefile.CaseFile("brief", {"tender_reference": "TEST-0001", "scenario_date": "2030-01-01"})
    facts.agents.update({"erp", "mail"})
    facts.merge("positions", {"positions": [{"position": "1", "quantity": 4, "requirement_ref": "REQ-1"}]})
    facts.merge("revisions", {"revisions": [{"revision": "B", "status": "current", "date": "2029-12-01"}]})
    row = {"requirement_ref": "REQ-1", "bore_mm": 50, "stroke_mm": stroke, "pressure_bar": 160, "mounting": "flange",
           "catalogue_group": "G-1", **requirement}
    facts.merge("requirements", {"revision": "B", "requirements": [row]})
    return facts


def material(stroke: int) -> dict:
    return {"materials": [{"material_number": "M-1", "catalogue_group": "G-1", "is_active": True, "bore_mm": 50,
                           "stroke_mm": stroke, "pressure_bar": 160, "mounting": "flange"}]}


def question(facts: casefile.CaseFile, qid: str) -> str:
    return dict(facts.questions()).get(qid, "")


class ChangedRequirement(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_a_later_amendment_is_told_to_every_agent_and_stays_in_the_open_question(self):
        facts = case()
        self.assertIn("stroke 207 mm", question(facts, "material:REQ-1"))
        self.assertNotIn("NOTE", question(facts, "material:REQ-1"))
        facts.take_news("erp"), facts.take_news("mail")

        facts.merge("clarifications", AMENDMENT)

        self.assertEqual(facts.changed, {"REQ-1": ["stroke 207 -> 200"]})
        for agent in ("erp", "mail"):
            news = facts.take_news(agent)
            self.assertEqual(len(news), 1, news)
            self.assertIn("CHANGED FACT: requirement REQ-1", news[0])
            self.assertIn("stroke 207 -> 200", news[0])
            self.assertIn("stroke 200 mm", news[0])
            self.assertIn("also a candidate that was ruled out", news[0])
        asked = question(facts, "material:REQ-1")
        self.assertIn("stroke 200 mm", asked)
        self.assertIn("NOTE: this requirement changed while you were working (stroke 207 -> 200)", asked)
        self.assertEqual(json.loads(facts.dump())["changed"], facts.changed)

    def test_an_absent_given_for_the_old_values_no_longer_counts(self):
        facts = case()
        facts.merge("material", material(stroke=200))  # the only material of the group: no match at stroke 207
        self.assertIn("closed as absent", facts.answer("material:REQ-1", "absent", "the only one has stroke 200"))
        self.assertEqual(facts.inputs().no_material, {"REQ-1"})

        facts.merge("clarifications", AMENDMENT)

        self.assertNotIn("material:REQ-1", facts.answers)
        self.assertEqual(facts.inputs().no_material, set())
        self.assertIn("material:REQ-1 was for the old values and no longer counts", facts.take_news("erp")[-1])
        self.assertNotIn("material:REQ-1", dict(facts.questions()))  # and the material on file is the match now
        self.assertIn("data:M-1", dict(facts.questions()))

    def test_an_absent_stays_open_again_until_a_match_is_filed(self):
        facts = case()
        facts.merge("material", material(stroke=300))
        facts.answer("material:REQ-1", "absent", "the only one has stroke 300")
        facts.merge("clarifications", AMENDMENT)
        self.assertIn("NOTE: this requirement changed", question(facts, "material:REQ-1"))

    def test_a_first_value_and_a_repeated_value_are_no_change(self):
        # a usable travel waits for its reserve: nobody was asked to match it yet, so its first value is no change
        facts = case(stroke=180, stroke_is_usable_travel=True, reserve_key="ER-1")
        self.assertEqual(question(facts, "material:REQ-1"), "")
        facts.merge("mail", {"messages": [{"sender": "tech@bidder.example", "timestamp": "2029-12-10T09:00:00Z",
                                           "subject": "release", "tender_reference": "TEST-0001",
                                           "tech_release": [{"revision": "B", "reserve_key": "ER-1",
                                                             "reserve_mm_per_end": 10}]}]})
        self.assertIn("stroke 200 mm", question(facts, "material:REQ-1"))
        facts.merge("requirements", {"revision": "B", "requirements": [
            {"requirement_ref": "REQ-1", "bore_mm": "50", "mounting": "Flange"}]})  # the same values, filed again
        self.assertEqual(facts.changed, {})
        self.assertEqual(facts.take_news("erp"), [])

    def test_only_the_values_that_moved_are_named(self):
        facts = case()
        facts.merge("requirements", {"revision": "B", "requirements": [
            {"requirement_ref": "REQ-1", "pressure_bar": 210, "mounting": "foot"}]})
        self.assertEqual(facts.changed["REQ-1"], ["pressure 160 -> 210", "mounting flange -> foot"])


class Languages(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_every_agent_and_the_extraction_are_told_that_pages_come_in_german_and_english(self):
        for text in (worker.ACTIONS_HELP, casefile.EXTRACT_SYSTEM):
            self.assertIn("German", text)
            self.assertIn("English", text)
            self.assertIn("translate", text)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

The test run of the branch scored **quality 44.9** (eligible, signed, 15:00, $0.20), and it tells us nothing about the two changes either way.

## What happened in the run

- **It ran out of model time.** Nine model calls got no reply within 120 to 150 seconds, including the very first one, so the investigation made only 139 calls (the 100 run made 260).
- **The ERP agent was cut off at the deadline and the mail agent did not finish.** The metal index was never filed, so the three priced positions have no surcharge, and the materials for two requirements were not resolved, so two positions were left out.
- **Load probably played a part.** Five to six runs were in flight under the shared model limit at the time. One of them still scored 100 in 9:34, so load is likely but not proven as the cause.

## What it says about my changes

- **Changed-fact notice:** it never fired, because no requirement changed after the agents had seen it in this run. The local tests cover it on constructed cases: every agent is told, the open question keeps saying it, and an "absent" given for the old values is reopened.
- **Language note:** one run cannot show an effect.
- **Nothing broke:** the bid was entered, signed and confirmed. All 300 local tests pass, 6 of them new.

## Where things stand

- **Nothing is committed or pushed, and `main` is untouched.**
- **The changes exist only as uncommitted edits** in a temporary working copy for the local branch `vamshidhar/changed-facts-and-language` (based on `main` at `4f3f572`). They touch `casefile.py`, `worker.py` and `agent.py`, plus one new test file.
- **A second scored submission is running right now** (`run_c4f64b7b`). It is the package that scored 100 once with Maria's loop fix. I did not start it.
- **The spread is still wide:** another package scored 100 and 15 in two runs while mine was going.

Uncommitted work in a temporary folder is easy to lose. May I commit it to that branch only, not to `main`?

# Coordinating Deep Research

## Your Role

You are acting as the **coordinator**. Your job is to analyze the user's question, spawn subagents, and manage output files. In order to keep your context clean, you should never conduct research or write files directly. For the same reason, you also should not read the researcher.md or report-writer.md files.

As you work, if you have a to-do or task-list tool (for example TodoWrite, or TaskCreate and TaskUpdate), use it to keep the user informed of your plan and progress. For clarity, don't reference subagents in those items. For example, you might say "Conduct research" instead of "Spawn research subagents".

## Process

1. [If necessary] Ask the user follow up questions
2. Choose a title for this research and create its directories
3. Decompose the user's query to determine subagent count
4. Spawn research subagents (in parallel)
5. [If absolutely necessary] Conduct one additional round of research
6. Spawn report writer subagent
7. Deliver report to user

### 1. [If necessary] Ask the user follow up questions

Read the user's question and consider if there are any missing or ambiguous details that need to be clarified. Some examples include:
- Ambiguous terminology — Acronyms, jargon, or terms with multiple meanings across different fields
- Implicit geographic or jurisdictional context — Questions where the answer varies significantly by region but no region is specified
- Ambiguous entities — Company names, product names, or proper nouns that refer to multiple distinct entities

In order to avoid creating unnecessary friction with the user, follow ups should only be asked when they would meaningfully impact how research is conducted.

If you determine that you do need to ask follow up questions, do so with the AskUserQuestion tool.

### 2. Choose a title for this research and create its directories

First choose a title for this research. It names the folder that will hold this request's research notes and is also the filename of the report the user receives, where it is shown as the report's title, so make it a short, specific title for this research in the user's language and in sentence case: 3 to 6 words and under 50 characters (count them, and drop words rather than exceed either limit), using only letters, numbers and single spaces. Keep accented and non-Latin letters exactly as the user's language writes them (for example é, ñ, ü, 日本語) rather than converting them to plain ASCII, and use no hyphens, underscores, apostrophes or other punctuation. For example, a question about how the EU AI Act affects startups could use "EU AI Act startup obligations".

This research's folders go in the same directory you used for research earlier in this conversation, or, if this is the first research request here, in your current working directory (not /tmp or an uploads folder). Before settling on the title, recall the titles of any research reports you have already delivered earlier in this conversation, and, if a research_notes/ folder already exists in that directory, list it — each folder inside it holds the notes behind a report of the same name in reports/, possibly from an earlier conversation. Then pick the case that fits:
- New topic: choose a fresh title.
- Returning to, extending or updating an earlier topic: choose a title that still names the topic and says what this request adds or changes (for example "EU AI Act startup penalties", not just "Penalties"), or, if nothing distinguishes it from the earlier request, the earlier title with the next number added, dropping a word first if that would exceed the limits above (for example "EU AI Act startup obligations 2"). Note the path of the most recent earlier report on that topic and of its notes folder: you will pass them to the report writer in step 6 as background to build on. If that report or its notes folder is no longer on disk, pass on only what remains and research whatever is missing.
- The user asks for earlier research to be redone independently: choose a title as in the previous case, but do not pass the earlier material on.

In every case the title must differ from every report delivered earlier in this conversation and from every folder you see, so that this request's notes and report never mix with or replace an earlier one's. Never rename, move or write into an earlier request's folder.

Then create the folders research_notes/{research title}/ and reports/ in that directory. Quote these paths in shell commands, since the title contains spaces, and note the directory's absolute path — you will give the subagents absolute paths into these folders, and they will store their files there.

### 3. Decompose the user's query to determine subagent count

In order to effectively spawn and task subagents, determine if and how the user's question can be decomposed into independent subtopics. These subtopics should be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. For each subtopic, then consider if the research requires (or would benefit from) multiple independent points of view.

| Researchers | Decomposition Strategy | Example |
|-------------|------------------------|---------|
| 1 | No meaningful decomposition — single factual question | "Who won the 2024 Super Bowl?" |
| 3 | Few natural angles or perspectives on a focused topic | "Effects of temperature on salmon migration" → (1) biological mechanisms, (2) observed population data, (3) climate projections |
| 4 | Distinct facets or evaluation criteria | "Compare CRM platforms for small businesses" → (1) pricing models, (2) feature comparison, (3) integrations ecosystem, (4) user reviews/sentiment |
| 5 | Multiple independent entities, regions, or domains | "AI regulation landscape" → (1) US federal, (2) EU/GDPR-AI Act, (3) China, (4) UK, (5) industry self-regulation |
| 6+ | Large enumerable set requiring systematic coverage | "Electric vehicle adoption rates by US state" → researchers assigned to regional clusters |

In the next step, you should spawn one subagent for each subtopic and independent point of view that you identified. When in doubt, 3 researchers is a reasonable default. If in step 2 you noted earlier research to build on, decompose only what this request adds or needs re-checked; the report writer will have the earlier material.

### 4. Spawn foreground research subagents (in parallel)

For each subtopic and independent point of view determined above, spawn a foreground research subagent.

To spawn research subagents, use the Agent tool (named Task in some versions) with subagent_type="general-purpose" and run_in_background=false. Ensure that you provide **extremely clear, specific** instructions to each research subagent. Be sure to propagate constraints of the original question to the research subagent (e.g., temporal, geographical). In the prompts below, replace {path_to_skill} with this skill's base directory (the directory this SKILL.md was loaded from), {absolute path of your working directory} with the path you noted in step 2, and {research title} with the title you chose in step 2. Follow the exact format provided below:

```
Agent(
  run_in_background=false
  subagent_type="general-purpose",
  description="{3-5 words}",
  prompt="Research {specific narrow topic}.

Objective: {clear description of what's covered in the desired output}

Key questions:
- {Specific question 1}
- {Specific question 2}

Suggested sources:
- {Types of source to prioritize}

Constraints:
- {Any bounds from the initial user query, including temporal or geographic}

Save your output notes to {absolute path of your working directory}/research_notes/{research title}/{topic}.md

**As a first step, you must read {path_to_skill}/references/researcher.md for instructions on how to conduct research.**"
)
```

Example of a good, clear, detailed prompt for a research subagent:

> Research the semiconductor supply chain crisis and its current status as of 2026.
>
> Objective: Compile a dense report of the facts, covering the current situation, ongoing solutions, and future outlook, with specific timelines and quantitative data where available.
>
> Key questions:
>  - What are current bottlenecks?
>  - What are the projected capacity increases from new fab construction?
>  - What are geopolitical factors affecting supply chains?
>  - When do experts predict supply will meet demand?
>
> Suggested sources:
> - Recent quarterly reports from major chip manufacturers like TSMC, Samsung, and Intel, found on investor relations pages or through the SEC EDGAR database
> - Industry reports from SEMI, Gartner, and IDC that provide market analysis and forecasts
> - Government responses, including US CHIPS Act implementation progress at commerce.gov, EU Chips Act at ec.europa.eu, and similar initiatives in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan through their respective government portals
>
> Constraints:
> - Must reflect current state as of 2026 with prior issues clearly noted as such
>
> Save your output notes to {absolute path of your working directory}/research_notes/Semiconductor supply chain outlook 2026/semiconductor_supply_chain.md
>
> **As a first step, you must read {path_to_skill}/references/researcher.md for instructions on how to conduct research.**"

In order to ensure research is conducted as quickly as possible, it's essential that all subagents are spawned in parallel, i.e., that you make all your calls to the Agent tool in a single turn.

### 5. [If absolutely necessary] Conduct one additional round of research

Based on the task summaries returned by the research subagents, determine if there are any critical gaps that would make the report incomplete. If deemed absolutely necessary, spawn researchers in parallel to close those gaps. Spawning additional researchers in this step delays delivery of the report to the user, leading to a much worse experience, so this must be used with extreme care.

**This step can only be followed once** - after the researchers finish, move immediately to Step 6, regardless of what results you get back. If you kick off any more research, you will hit timeouts or rate limits, meaning the user will never get an answer to their query. **To help yourself remember this, you should always output "After these researchers finish, I will move directly to coordinating the report writer" when choosing to kick off additional research.**

### 6. Spawn foreground report writer subagent

After research is done, spawn a single report writer subagent. Use the Agent tool (named Task in some versions) with subagent_type="general-purpose" and run_in_background=false, and fill in the placeholders as in step 4. For {the user's original question}, state the question this report must answer in full — if this request returns to or extends earlier research, that is the earlier question as amended by this request (for example "How does the EU AI Act affect startups, including penalties?"), not just the follow-up message. On the line for earlier research, give the absolute paths of the earlier report and notes folder you noted in step 2, or write "none" if you noted nothing to build on or the user asked for an independent redo. Follow the exact format provided below:

```
Agent(
  run_in_background=false
  subagent_type="general-purpose",
  description="Write final report",
  prompt="Read the notes in {absolute path of your working directory}/research_notes/{research title}/ and synthesize into a research report that answers: {the user's original question}.

Earlier research in this conversation to build on: {absolute paths of the earlier report and notes folder from step 2, or "none"}

Save your final report to this exact path: {absolute path of your working directory}/reports/{research title}.md

**As a first step, you must read {path_to_skill}/references/report-writer.md for instructions on how to write your research report.**"
)
```

### 7. Deliver report to user

After the report writer is done, make the report available to the user: if you have a tool for sending files to the user (for example SendUserFile), send reports/{research title}.md with it; otherwise, if your environment has a user-visible outputs folder, copy the report there under the same filename; otherwise leave it at reports/{research title}.md. Then read the finalized report and send the user a brief summary (aim for 3-5 sentences) that says where the full report is (sent to them, in the outputs folder, or its absolute path).


ARGUMENTS: Research goal: find different and better agent architectures and techniques (from research papers and strong open systems) to make a multi-website, model-directed web agent reliable under a 20-minute limit, then apply them. Context: TUM/Atira "From RFQ to bid" challenge; same code scores 100, 44.9, 38.2, 15 and 10 across runs; failures are agents looping or acting on stale facts, late facts, and model-call timeouts.

"""Specialized investigators wake only for questions their portal can answer."""
import asyncio
import sys
import time
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

from agent import Team, questions_for_site  # noqa: E402


class FakeCase:
    def __init__(self):
        self.version = 0
        self.pending = 0
        self.news = {}
        self.open_questions = [("mailbox", "Find the sales mailbox.")]
        self.changed = asyncio.Event()

    def questions(self):
        return list(self.open_questions)

    async def wait_change(self, seen, timeout):
        if self.version == seen:
            try:
                await asyncio.wait_for(self.changed.wait(), timeout)
            except asyncio.TimeoutError:
                return False
            self.changed.clear()
        return self.version != seen

    def update(self, question):
        self.open_questions.append(question)
        self.version += 1
        self.changed.set()


class QuestionRouting(unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase):
    def test_erp_and_mail_receive_only_resolvable_questions(self):
        questions = [
            ("positions", "Find tender positions."),
            ("material:REQ-1", "Find a matching ERP material."),
            ("data:MAT-1", "Find missing ERP data."),
            ("discount", "Find discount approval."),
            ("reserve:REQ-2", "Find technical release."),
        ]

        self.assertEqual([qid for qid, _ in questions_for_site("erp", questions)],
                         ["material:REQ-1", "data:MAT-1"])
        self.assertEqual([qid for qid, _ in questions_for_site("mail", questions)],
                         ["discount", "reserve:REQ-2"])
        self.assertEqual(questions_for_site("new-portal", questions), questions)

    async def test_erp_idle_hook_ignores_new_mail_questions(self):
        case = FakeCase()
        team = Team(case, ["erp"], time.time() + 5)
        hook = team.hook("erp")
        waiting = asyncio.create_task(hook("done"))
        await asyncio.sleep(0)

        case.update(("discount", "Find discount approval."))
        await asyncio.sleep(0.02)
        self.assertFalse(waiting.done())

        case.update(("material:REQ-1", "Find a matching ERP material."))
        self.assertIn("material:REQ-1", await waiting)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

input.description: Research loop and stall recovery
input.prompt:
Research stall, loop and perseveration detection and recovery in LLM agents (especially web/browser agents driven by small, fast models), as of October 2026.

Objective: Compile dense, citable notes on the mechanisms published agent systems and papers use to (a) notice that an agent is not making progress, (b) get it out of the rut, and (c) avoid the rut in the first place, with the measured effect where reported. The notes must end with concrete algorithms or pseudocode that could be added to an existing Python observe-think-act loop within a few hours.

Background you need (the system these findings will be applied to):
- A hackathon agent system must, inside a 20-minute run, gather facts from four enterprise-style websites (tender portal, supplier portal with a paged specification, SAP-like ERP, webmail), apply deterministic pricing rules, fill a bid form and sign it. One LLM "investigator" loop runs per website in parallel: it sees the page as accessibility-style text, replies with a short thought plus up to 8 actions (click, fill, goto, collect a paged list, file the page as evidence, close an open question), and keeps only its last 2 turns verbatim (older turns are compressed to the action results). A shared case file lists OPEN QUESTIONS that are recomputed every turn from missing facts.
- The model is Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a fast open-weight model used WITHOUT its thinking mode for navigation (about 3 s per call). A second, cheap decision model (Cloudflare Clef: pick one of N options, yes-probability, or a score, from text plus up to 4 screenshots) is available.
- Observed failures on identical code (scores 100, 100, 44.9, 38.2, 15, 10): an agent clicked a vanished element 78 times in a row although each result said the element no longer exists; an agent cycled through the same four search queries for 65 steps; an agent re-ran one search for 46 turns while repeating the same sentence as its thought ("X has stroke 500, not 507") although the shared state had been corrected minutes earlier; an agent kept reloading a mailbox because it distrusted a label. A text warning "you have sent the same actions three times" was already injected and was ignored.
- Rules of the competition: the model must choose navigation, searches and documents at run time. Deterministic helpers may validate, retry, block, restart, paginate and extract, but may not crawl the sites on their own or encode knowledge of the public sites. The final evaluation uses different websites.

Key questions:
- Which published systems track progress explicitly and replan on stalls, and how exactly? Cover at least Magentic-One (task ledger, progress ledger, stall counter, replanning), AutoGen/Magentic-UI, Reflexion, ReAct failure analyses, LATS, Agent-E (change observation), AgentOccam, WebPilot, SteP, SWE-agent/OpenHands guardrails (for example stuck detection in OpenHands), BrowserGym/AgentLab studies, and any 2025-2026 work on "agent loops", "repetition", "perseveration" or "stuck detection". Quote the actual thresholds and prompts where the source gives them.
- What is known about WHY small or non-reasoning models repeat (copying their own previous output from context, history formatting, lack of state change signals), and which context/history designs reduce it (removing the previous thought, summarising history as a list of tried-and-failed actions, tabu lists, showing a diff of the page instead of the page)?
- Hard interventions versus soft hints: evidence on refusing to execute a repeated action, forcing a choice among untried alternatives (possibly chosen by a separate decision model), resetting or restarting the agent with a fresh context and a summary, or handing the subgoal to another agent. Which work, and what are their failure modes?
- Detection signals beyond exact repetition: n-gram cycles of actions, no change in the page fingerprint, no new evidence filed in N steps, same thought text, time since last progress. Which are used in practice and with what thresholds?
- How do strong systems phrase an intervention so that the model actually changes course?

Suggested sources:
- arXiv papers and their official code repositories (read the code for thresholds: for example microsoft/autogen Magentic-One orchestrator, All-Hands-AI/OpenHands stuck detector, ServiceNow/AgentLab, web-arena-x).
- Benchmark papers with failure taxonomies: WebArena, VisualWebArena, WorkArena and WorkArena++, AssistantBench, OSWorld and OSWorld-Verified, tau-bench, and "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" (MAST).

input.description: Research coordination and routing
input.prompt:
Research architectures and coordination schemes for several LLM agents that gather interdependent facts from different sources in parallel under a hard deadline, as of October 2026.

Objective: Compile dense, citable notes on how to coordinate parallel agents over a shared state so that (a) each agent works only on what its source can answer, without that assignment being hard-coded, (b) facts that depend on other agents' findings are scheduled sensibly, and (c) no agent keeps acting on a fact that another agent has since corrected. The notes must end with concrete designs or pseudocode that fit an existing Python system and can be built in a few hours.

Background you need (the system these findings will be applied to):
- A hackathon agent system must, inside a 20-minute run, gather facts from four enterprise-style websites (a tender portal with a bill of quantities and a bidder Q&A, a supplier portal with a paged technical specification and its revisions, a SAP-like ERP with materials, stock and price conditions, and a webmail with approvals, tariffs and a signing code), apply 29 deterministic pricing rules, fill a bid form and sign it. One LLM "investigator" loop runs per website in parallel (model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, fast, no thinking mode, about 3 s per call; up to 32 concurrent calls).
- A shared case file (a blackboard) holds typed records that a separate extraction call produces from pages an agent files. OPEN QUESTIONS are derived deterministically from the missing facts (for example "material for requirement R: bore, stroke, pressure ..." appears only once the requirement is known, and "reserve for R" once a requirement turns out to need one). Every agent sees the full case-file summary and all open questions at the head of every turn. A finished agent sleeps and is woken when a new question appears.
- Measured: identical code scored 100, 100, 44.9, 38.2, 15 and 10. In bad runs: the ERP agent searched blindly for 45 turns while the requirements had not arrived yet; it rejected the right material for 46 turns because a requirement value was corrected later by another agent's filing and it never noticed; the mail agent searched one folder only; an idle agent was not woken because its question was not "new". A variant in which each agent sees only the questions its own website can answer scored 100 in 9.5 minutes with every agent finishing by itself, but that routing is keyed on the public site names ("erp", "mail").
- Rules of the competition: a model must choose navigation, searches and documents at run time; deterministic code may schedule, validate, notify, retry and extract. The final evaluation uses DIFFERENT websites: other software, layout, navigation and site names, and the information may be split differently across the sites. Nothing may be tuned to the public sites.

Key questions:
- Orchestrator-worker versus peer blackboard versus hybrid: what do published systems use and what does the evidence say for information-gathering tasks with dependencies? Cover Magentic-One, AutoGen group chat and its successors, MetaGPT and its shared message pool, LangGraph supervisor and swarm patterns, CrewAI flows, Anthropic's multi-agent research system write-up, OpenAI Agents SDK handoffs, and recent LLM blackboard papers (for example blackboard systems for information discovery, 2025).
- Capability discovery and dynamic routing: how can a system learn at run time which source can answer which kind of question (source profiling or "site cards" written by the agent after a first look, capability registries, contract-net style bidding, routing by retrieval over source descriptions, asking each agent to claim questions with a confidence)? What published evidence exists, and what goes wrong (missed questions, double work)? Give a design that degrades safely when the profile is wrong.
- Dependency-aware scheduling: representing missing facts as a task graph, releasing a question only when its inputs are stable, speculative work on likely-needed items, and what an agent should do while blocked (nothing, pre-navigate, cache candidate pages). What do systems such as LLMCompiler, ReWOO, plan-and-execute agents and data-agent blackboards do?
- Stale beliefs: how do multi-agent systems propagate state changes (versioned facts, push notifications, invalidating conclusions derived from old values, truth maintenance, re-grounding on the current state each turn)? Include classic blackboard and truth-maintenance ideas where they translate directly, clearly marked as background.
- Failure taxonomies for multi-agent LLM systems ("Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" MAST and follow-ups): which failure categories match the ones above and which mitigations were measured?
- Wake-up and termination: how to decide that the team is done, and how to avoid both early termination and idle waiting.

Suggested sources:
- arXiv papers and official repositories of the systems named above; Microsoft Research, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, LangChain and Berkeley (MAST) write-ups from 2024-2026.
- Classic references only as background: Hearsay-II and blackboard systems, contract net protocol, truth maintenance systems.

Constraints:
- Prefer 2024-2026 sources; mark older work as background. State clearly when something is your inference rather than a reported result.
- Recommendations must not depend on knowing the websites in advance, must keep the model in charge of navigation, and must be implementable in hours on top of the described system.

input.description: Research reliability and latency
input.prompt:
Research reliability engineering and variance reduction for LLM agent systems that must finish inside a fixed time limit, as of October 2026.

Objective: Compile dense, citable notes on why the same agent code gives very different results from run to run, and on the engineering measures that make every run land close to the best one: handling slow and hung model calls, deadline-aware control, redundancy and verification at the few decisions that matter, restart strategies, and how to measure reliability with few runs. The notes must end with concrete measures (with pseudocode where useful) that can be added to an existing Python asyncio system in a few hours, each with its expected benefit and its cost in model calls and time.

Background you need (the system these findings will be applied to):
- A hackathon agent system must, inside a 20-minute scored run, gather facts from four enterprise-style websites with four parallel LLM agent loops, extract typed records from the pages they file (a separate LLM call per page), compute a bid with deterministic code, then fill a web form and sign it with a one-time code fetched from a webmail. Ranking: eligible first, then quality 0-100, then lower cost x time. A partial bid that is signed scores its filled positions; an unsigned bid scores nothing.
- Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next through an OpenAI-compatible proxy, about 3 s per call at the median, a p95 near 9 s, and a shared limit of 32 concurrent calls per team across all runs. The client currently waits up to 120-150 s for a reply and retries. A cheap decision model (Cloudflare Clef: choice, yes-probability or score) is also available, and frontier models through a metered proxy if worth their cost.
- Measured on the same public scenario with the same or nearly the same code: 100, 100, 100, 44.9, 38.2, 15, 10. A good run needs about 200-260 model calls and finishes the investigation in 5-8 minutes; the form and signature take about 4 minutes. In one bad run 9 calls got no reply within 120-150 s (the very first call included), so the investigation made 139 calls instead of 260 and ran into its deadline. In others one agent looped until the deadline. The investigation is cut off 8 minutes before the end to leave time for the form and the signature.
- Rules: a model must choose navigation, searches and documents; deterministic code may retry, time out, hedge, schedule, validate and restart. The final evaluation runs once (or best of three) on different websites.

Key questions:
- Tail latency: what do "The Tail at Scale" (Dean and Barroso), hedged and tied requests, backup requests with a short delay, adaptive timeouts based on observed percentiles, and retry budgets recommend, and how have LLM applications applied them (hedging LLM calls, cancelling the loser, per-call timeouts tuned to output length)? What timeout and hedge delay are sensible for a call whose p50 is 3 s and p95 is 9 s? What are the costs when concurrency is capped?
- Variance and reliability measurement: pass^k from tau-bench and tau2-bench, reliability findings in "AI Agents That Matter" (Kapoor et al.), HAL, and 2025-2026 studies on run-to-run variance of agents at temperature 0. How many runs are needed to tell an 80 % reliable system from a 95 % one, and what cheap proxies exist (per-stage success rates, replay of saved pages)?
- Deadline-aware control: anytime algorithms and budgeted planning for agents (step budgets per subgoal, budget-aware prompts, early stopping, saving a partial result early and improving it), and evidence that telling a model its remaining budget changes behaviour. How should the split between investigation and submission be set and adapted during the run?
- Redundancy at decision points: self-consistency and majority voting, verifier or critic models, dual extraction with comparison, running a second agent on the same subtask from a different start (portfolio or racing strategies), and what the literature says about when redundancy helps versus when errors are correlated.
- Restart and recovery: checkpoint and restart of an agent with a summary, supervisor timeouts per subgoal, "restart beats continue" results (for example restarts in search algorithms and in SWE agents), and how to preserve what the agent already learned.
- Determinism: temperature, seeds, prompt caching and ordering effects; does lowering temperature reduce harmful variance for navigation, and what do model providers and papers report?

Suggested sources:
- Systems literature: Dean and Barroso 2013 (background), Google SRE book chapters on handling overload and retries (background), recent engineering posts on LLM request hedging and timeouts.
- Agent evaluation literature 2024-2026: tau-bench, tau2-bench, "AI Agents That Matter", HAL (Holistic Agent Leaderboard), OSWorld-Verified, WebArena-Verified, BrowserGym/AgentLab reproducibility studies.
- Papers on budget-aware or deadline-aware agents, self-consistency (Wang et al.), multi-agent verification, and restart strategies.

Constraints:
- Prefer 2024-2026 sources for agent-specific claims; classic systems papers are fine as background and must be marked as such. State clearly when a number is your own estimate.
- Measures must be implementable in hours in Python asyncio with an OpenAI-compatible client, and must respect the shared concurrency limit.
- Time budget: about 15 minutes of research.

211	## 7. Which concrete measures can be added to the existing Python asyncio system in a few hours, with expected benefit and cost?
212	
213	### Takeaway
214	Eight measures, ordered by expected benefit per hour of work: bounded and hedged model calls behind one concurrency governor, a start-up canary, a live deadline controller with an anytime bid, a stall-and-loop supervisor that restarts with a summary, redundancy only at extraction and at the "done" decision, and a measurement harness with fault injection. In a normal run they add roughly 15-25 % model calls and no wall time; in a bad run they are the difference between a full signed bid and a partial one.
215	
216	### Cited Findings
217	- Hedge after the 95th percentile for about 5 % extra load; cancel the loser. — [Dean and Barroso 2013](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)
218	- At most three attempts per request and a retry budget of about 10 % of requests; retry at one layer only; shed low-criticality work first. — [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
219	- For LLM calls, time the hedge on the first token, cap hedges at 5-10 % of traffic, and be careful behind a shared rate limit. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/); [Tian Pan](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
220	- A per-step budget block with tiers changes agent behaviour; verification of each constraint and summary-based context refresh add further gains. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
221	- Clear the context before a retry. — [Yang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)
222	- Same-model repeats share errors; agreement is a better doubt signal than a vote. — [Kim et al. 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/kim25e.html); [Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
223	- Measure reliability over repeated trials (pass^k) and under injected faults. — [tau-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045); [ReliabilityBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06112v1)
224	
225	### Inferences
226	
227	All benefit and cost numbers in this section are my own estimates, based on the simulation in question 1 and a good run of 200-260 calls.
228	
229	#### Summary table
230	
231	| # | Measure | Failure it removes | Expected benefit | Extra model calls | Extra wall time | Work |
232	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
233	| 1 | Cap each attempt at 20-30 s, one backup after about 8 s, cancel loser, max 3 rounds, SDK retries off | Hung calls eating the window (the 139-call run) | Model wait per agent at 6 % hangs: about 780 s down to about 260-270 s; no harm at 0 % | +5 % on a healthy day, up to +22 % on a bad one (10-55 calls) | none; saves minutes in bad runs | 1-1.5 h |
234	| 2 | One concurrency governor: semaphore of 28, hedges limited to 4 slots and 20 % of calls, agent steps before extraction | Self-inflicted queueing at the limit of 32; hedge storms | Removes one possible cause of hangs; keeps hedging safe | 0 | none | 30 min |
235	| 3 | Canary at start: 3 parallel one-token calls, first reply wins | "The very first call got no reply" | Saves up to 150 s at the start; gives a health reading | 3 | none (runs during browser start) | 15 min |
236	| 4 | Budget block after every step plus code-side step budgets per required item | Agents wandering; one item eating the window | In the source study: same accuracy at about 31 % lower cost; here mainly earlier finish | 0 (about 40 tokens per step) | none | 45 min |
237	| 5 | Live reserve for submission, early stop when the checklist is complete, bid recomputed on every new record | Running into the cut-off; unsigned or thin bid | Signature protected on slow days; up to 2 minutes returned on normal days; better time tie-breaker | 0 | none | 1-2 h |
238	| 6 | Supervisor: stall and loop detection, restart with a fresh context and a code-built summary, max 2 restarts per site | "One agent looped until the deadline" | Turns a lost site into a 1-2 minute delay | 0 in good runs; 5-15 per restart | 0 in good runs | 1-1.5 h |
239	| 7 | Dual extraction on bid-relevant pages with field comparison; decision-model gate on "done"; deterministic validation | Silent extraction errors; premature "done" | Catches non-shared errors on the values that set the score | +15 to +40, plus a few cheap decision calls | about 0 if parallel, else one call (3-9 s) | 1.5-2 h |
240	| 8 | Call log, replay of saved pages, fault-injection wrapper | Flying blind with 3-7 runs | Hundreds of samples per hour; proves measures 1 and 6 work before the final | offline only | none in scored runs | 1-1.5 h |

244	#### Measure 1 and 2: bounded, hedged calls behind one governor
245	
246	```python
247	import asyncio, collections, random, time
248	
249	class Deadline:
250	    def __init__(self, seconds): self.t_end = time.monotonic() + seconds
251	    def left(self): return self.t_end - time.monotonic()
252	
253	class LatencyStats:                              # one per call type: "step", "extract", "form"
254	    def __init__(self, default=8.0, lo=5.0, hi=12.0, n=60):
255	        self.buf = collections.deque(maxlen=n); self.default, self.lo, self.hi = default, lo, hi
256	    def add(self, s): self.buf.append(s)
257	    def hedge_delay(self):                       # rolling p90, clamped
258	        if len(self.buf) < 20: return self.default
259	        xs = sorted(self.buf)
260	        return min(self.hi, max(self.lo, xs[int(0.9 * (len(xs) - 1))]))
261	
262	LLM_SLOTS   = asyncio.Semaphore(28)              # team limit is 32: keep headroom
263	HEDGE_SLOTS = asyncio.Semaphore(4)               # backups may never hold more than 4 slots
264	
265	class HedgeBudget:                               # at most ~20 % extra calls (a 6 % hang rate plus the p90 rule needs ~16-20 %)
266	    def __init__(self): self.calls = 0; self.hedges = 0
267	    def primary(self): self.calls += 1
268	    def try_take(self):
269	        if self.hedges + 1 <= 0.20 * self.calls + 3: self.hedges += 1; return True
270	        return False
271	HEDGES = HedgeBudget()
272	
273	class LLMUnavailable(Exception): pass
274	
275	async def llm_call(make_request, *, kind, stats, deadline, cap=20.0, rounds=3, critical=False):
276	    """make_request() performs ONE HTTP call (client built with max_retries=0, timeout=cap+5).
277	    LLM calls have no side effects, so duplicates are safe; only the winner's action is executed."""
278	    for r in range(rounds):
279	        budget = min(cap, deadline.left() - 1.0)
280	        if budget < 2.0: break
281	        HEDGES.primary(); t0 = time.monotonic()
282	
283	        async def timed():                                       # the winner's OWN latency feeds the statistics
284	            t = time.monotonic(); res = await make_request(); return res, time.monotonic() - t
285	        async def primary():
286	            async with LLM_SLOTS: return await timed()
287	        async def backup():
288	            async with HEDGE_SLOTS, LLM_SLOTS: return await timed()
289	
290	        tasks = [asyncio.create_task(primary())]
291	        try:
292	            wait_first = 0.0 if critical else min(stats[kind].hedge_delay(), budget)
293	            done, _ = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=wait_first)
294	            if not done and (critical or HEDGES.try_take()):     # slow, not failed: add ONE backup, keep the primary
295	                tasks.append(asyncio.create_task(backup()))
296	            while True:
297	                good = [t for t in tasks if t.done() and not t.cancelled() and t.exception() is None]
298	                if good:
299	                    res, own = good[0].result()
300	                    stats[kind].add(own)
301	                    return res
302	                pending = [t for t in tasks if not t.done()]
303	                left = budget - (time.monotonic() - t0)
304	                if not pending or left <= 0: break               # all failed, or round cap reached
305	                await asyncio.wait(pending, timeout=left, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
306	        finally:
307	            for t in tasks: t.cancel()                           # cancel the loser: closes the connection, frees the slot
308	            await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
309	        await asyncio.sleep(random.random() * min(1.0, 0.25 * 2 ** r))   # short jittered pause
310	    raise LLMUnavailable(kind)
311	```
312	
313	- Settings: `cap` 20 s for agent steps, 25-30 s for extraction calls with long output; `critical=True` (backup sent at once) only for the handful of calls on the path to the signature. Set `max_tokens` on every call.
314	- If the proxy streams: inside `make_request` wrap the first chunk in `asyncio.wait_for(first_chunk, 8)` and raise on expiry. A call with no first token after 8 s is treated as hung, while a long answer that is flowing is left alone.
315	- Priority: agent-step calls take `LLM_SLOTS` directly; the page-extraction fan-out should pass through a second, smaller semaphore (for example 16) so that a burst of pages can never starve the four agent loops.
316	- Circuit breaker for a proxy-wide bad day: if more than about 15 % of the last 20 calls hit the round cap, send agent-step calls to the fallback model through the metered proxy until 10 consecutive probe calls to the main model succeed. Cost: money only in bad runs.
317	- Smoke test (own run, fake request function with the lognormal latency, 6 % hangs and 2 % errors, four loops of 65 calls): every logical call returned, the four loops took 250-264 simulated seconds each against about 242 s with no hangs at all, 316 requests were sent for 260 logical calls (+22 %), 50 losers were cancelled, and all slots were free at the end. The adaptive hedge delay settled at about 6 s.
318	- Pitfall found in that test: if the statistics record the time of the whole logical call instead of the winning attempt's own latency, every rescued hang adds an 11-plus-second sample, the p90 drifts up to the clamp of 12 s, and hedging gets slower exactly when it is needed. The code above records the winner's own latency for that reason.
319	- Cost check: +5 % calls with a fixed hedge at 9 s on a healthy proxy, up to about +22 % with the adaptive p90 rule on a day with 6 % hangs. With 4 loops and up to 16 extraction calls in flight, plus at most 4 backups, the peak is 24 concurrent calls, under the semaphore of 28.
320	
321	#### Measure 3: canary
322	
323	```python
324	async def canary(make_tiny_request, n=3, cap=10.0):
325	    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(make_tiny_request()) for _ in range(n)]     # max_tokens=1
326	    t0 = time.monotonic()
327	    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=cap, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
328	    for t in pending: t.cancel()
329	    return (time.monotonic() - t0) if done else None    # None -> start in degraded mode (fallback model, tighter budgets)
330	```
331	
332	#### Measures 4 and 5: deadline controller and anytime bid
333	
334	```python
335	RUN = Deadline(20 * 60)
336	
337	def submit_reserve(stats):                       # recomputed during the run
338	    p90 = stats["form"].hedge_delay()            # live latency of this run
339	    est = FORM_BROWSER_SECONDS + FORM_LLM_CALLS * p90 * 1.5      # both constants from test-run logs
340	    return max(330.0, est)                       # floor: slowest submission seen in tests + 60-90 s; 480 s until measured
341	
342	def investigation_left(stats): return RUN.left() - submit_reserve(stats)
343	
344	def budget_block(agent, stats):                  # appended after every tool result
345	    left = investigation_left(stats); frac = left / INVESTIGATION_SECONDS
346	    tier = "HIGH" if frac >= .7 else "MEDIUM" if frac >= .3 else "LOW" if frac >= .1 else "CRITICAL"
347	    return (f"<budget>steps used {agent.steps}/{agent.max_steps}; investigation time left {int(left)} s; "
348	            f"tier {tier}; still missing: {', '.join(agent.missing()) or 'nothing'}. "
349	            f"LOW: finish the most valuable missing item only. CRITICAL: file what you have and stop.</budget>")
350	
351	async def controller(agents, store, stats):
352	    while True:
353	        await asyncio.sleep(2)
354	        if store.changed(): store.bid = compute_bid(store.records)          # deterministic; always a submittable bid
355	        if store.checklist_complete() and store.verified(): break           # early stop: all required records present
356	        if investigation_left(stats) <= 0: break                            # hard cut-off
357	    for a in agents: a.cancel()
358	    await submit_and_sign(store.bid, deadline=RUN)                          # calls here use critical=True
359	```
360	
361	- The model still chooses every navigation step; code only tells it the time, enforces the stop, and computes the bid.
362	- Per-item step budgets: when an item on an agent's list has used its allowance (for example 12 steps), mark it unresolved in the block and require the agent to move to the next item.
363	- If the form allows it, open and pre-fill it in a second browser context once the first complete draft bid exists, so that only the final update and the signature remain after the cut-off.
364	
365	#### Measure 6: supervisor with clean restart
366	
367	```python
368	STARTS = ["navigate from the home page", "use the site search first", "start from the sitemap or footer links"]
369	
370	async def supervise(site, make_agent, store, stats, stall_s=75, max_restarts=2):
371	    for attempt in range(max_restarts + 1):
372	        if investigation_left(stats) < 60 or store.site_complete(site): return
373	        agent = make_agent(site, start_hint=STARTS[attempt % len(STARTS)],
374	                           summary=store.summary(site))        # built by code: records filed, URLs visited, dead ends
375	        task = asyncio.create_task(agent.run(store))           # fresh context: the old transcript is dropped
376	        while not task.done():
377	            await asyncio.wait([task], timeout=5)
378	            stalled = time.monotonic() - store.last_progress(site) > stall_s   # no new record or filed page
379	            looping = agent.same_action_repeats() >= 3                          # same tool+arguments or same URL
380	            if stalled or looping or investigation_left(stats) <= 0:
381	                task.cancel(); break
382	        await asyncio.gather(task, return_exceptions=True)
383	```
384	
385	- Set `stall_s` from logs: the longest gap between two filed pages in the runs that scored 100, times 1.5.
386	- Work stealing: when a site finishes early, call `supervise` a second time for the site with the most missing items, with a different start hint; both agents write to the same store. This uses slots that would otherwise sit idle.
387	- The store and the visited set are written at every step and flushed to disk at each stage, so a restart or crash loses nothing.
388	
389	#### Measure 7: redundancy only where it pays
390	
391	- Deterministic validation first, at no model cost: types, ranges, units, currency, totals across records, and required fields present. A failed check sends the page back to extraction once with the error named.
392	- Dual extraction for pages whose records feed the bid: second call with a different view of the page (structured table text versus raw text, or reversed section order) at the same time as the first; compare field by field in code; only disagreeing fields get a third opinion (frontier model through the metered proxy if a wrong value would cost more than the call).
393	- Decision-model gates, each a short call: "does this page contain a record of type X" before a document is filed or dropped, and "is every item on this checklist supported by a filed page" before an agent may declare itself done.
394	- No voting on ordinary navigation steps.
395	
396	#### Measure 8: measurement in few runs
397	
398	- Log one line per attempt: call type, start time, first-token time, total time, output tokens, outcome (ok, capped, backup won, cancelled), calls in flight. Log one line per stage with success and duration, and the slack in seconds at the cut-off and at the signature.
399	- Replay: store every filed page of a good run; run extraction and bid computation on the stored set 20 times and report per-field agreement and bid agreement. This is the stage-level pass^k.
400	- Fault injection wrapper around `make_request` for test runs: with probability 6 % sleep for 300 s (a hang), with probability 10 % multiply latency by 3, and once per run stall a whole agent for 90 s. Acceptance test before the final: three consecutive fault-injected runs that all sign a complete bid. Three runs cannot prove 95 % reliability (see question 2), but a fault-injected pass shows the two known failure modes are handled.
401	- For the final evaluation: make sure no other run of the team is active, since the 32-call limit is shared across runs.
402	
403	### Gaps
404	- All benefit figures here are estimates from a simulation with an assumed lognormal latency and independent hangs; real hangs may cluster in time, which lowers the benefit of hedging and raises the value of the fallback route.
405	- `FORM_BROWSER_SECONDS`, `FORM_LLM_CALLS`, the stall threshold and the number of bid-relevant pages must be read from the team's own run logs; I had no access to them.
406	- Whether dual extraction, the decision-model gates and work stealing stay within the challenge's fair-play rules is for the team to confirm against the rules text; they keep the model in charge of navigation, searches and document choice, which is the constraint stated in the brief.

"""The agents' model client: one JSON chat call to the hosted Qwen, built to survive a busy run.

Every decision the agents take goes through `chat_json`: JSON mode, thinking on or off per call, a cap on how many
calls run at once (the hosted model serves 32 per team across all its runs), retries with backoff and a tolerant
parse of the reply. It never raises: when the last attempt fails it returns {} and the caller decides how to go on
without an answer. `STATS` adds up calls, tokens and seconds; `summary` is the line a run prints at its end.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json
import os
import random
import re
import sys
import time

from openai import APIStatusError, AsyncOpenAI

MODEL = "qwen"
MAX_CONCURRENT = 16  # the team's limit is 32 across all its runs, and test runs may overlap
ATTEMPTS = 5
CALL_TIMEOUT = 150  # seconds: a model that scaled to zero is slow to answer its first call
WARM_TIMEOUT = 120  # a quick call (thinking off) this late once the model is awake is stuck: ask again. 75 s cut off
# a first turn with a large prompt under load (submit agent, sandbox test run 54c78c38: 85 s lost to the retry).
# Calls with thinking on (fact extraction) keep CALL_TIMEOUT: under load they legitimately take longer.
MAX_TOKENS_CEILING = 16000  # a reply cut off by its token limit is asked again with twice the room, up to this
PERMANENT = (400, 401, 403, 404, 413, 422)  # asking again rarely helps: one more try, then give up
# The hosted Qwen's simulated prices in USD per million tokens, for the estimate in `summary`.
PRICE_INPUT, PRICE_CACHED, PRICE_OUTPUT = 0.15, 0.016, 0.47
REMINDER = "That reply was not a single JSON object. Answer again with exactly one JSON object and nothing else."

STATS = {"calls": 0, "failed": 0, "prompt_tokens": 0, "cached_tokens": 0, "completion_tokens": 0, "seconds": 0.0}
BY_LABEL: dict[str, list] = {}  # caller kind -> [calls, seconds], to see where a run spends its time
_warm = {"done": False}

_bound: dict = {}  # the client and the gate belong to one event loop; another loop (tests) gets its own


def _load_local_env() -> None:
    """Local development only: KEY=VALUE lines from the repo root's .env.local (never shipped: it sits outside the
    package folder). Values already in the environment win. Nothing is printed."""
    path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), ".env.local")
    if not os.path.isfile(path):
        return
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        name, sep, value = line.strip().partition("=")
        if sep and name and not name.startswith("#"):
            os.environ.setdefault(name.strip(), value.strip().strip('"'))


_load_local_env()

# Fact extraction can go to OpenAI instead of the hosted Qwen: EXTRACT_PROVIDER=openai and OPENAI_MODEL=<model>.
# In a run, OPENAI_BASE_URL points at the metering proxy and the key is the team secret OPENAI_API_KEY.
OPENAI_MODEL = os.environ.get("OPENAI_MODEL", "")


def _session(provider: str = "qwen") -> tuple[AsyncOpenAI, asyncio.Semaphore]:
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()

    return None


def _count(usage, provider: str = "qwen") -> None:
    if usage is None:
        return
    if provider != "qwen":  # priced differently: kept apart from the Qwen estimate
        STATS[f"{provider}_tokens"] = STATS.get(f"{provider}_tokens", 0) + (usage.prompt_tokens or 0) + (usage.completion_tokens or 0)
        return
    STATS["prompt_tokens"] += usage.prompt_tokens or 0
    STATS["completion_tokens"] += usage.completion_tokens or 0
    STATS["cached_tokens"] += getattr(usage.prompt_tokens_details, "cached_tokens", None) or 0


async def chat_json(messages: list[dict], *, think: bool = True, max_tokens: int = 6000, label: str = "",
                    provider: str = "qwen") -> dict:
    """One chat call that answers with a JSON object. {} when every attempt failed; it never raises.

    `think` turns the model's reasoning on or off: off is about twice as fast, for the easy steps. `label` names the
    caller in the failure lines on stderr.
    """
    try:
        client, gate = _session(provider)
    except KeyError as missing:
        STATS["failed"] += 1
        print(f"[llm] {label or 'call'}: {missing} is not set, no model to ask", file=sys.stderr)
        return {}
    conversation = messages
    for attempt in range(1, ATTEMPTS + 1):
        permanent = False
        try:
            async with gate:
                STATS["calls"] += 1
                started = time.monotonic()
                try:
                    if provider == "openai":
                        request = client.chat.completions.create(
                            model=OPENAI_MODEL, messages=conversation, max_completion_tokens=max_tokens,
                            response_format={"type": "json_object"})
                    else:
                        request = client.chat.completions.create(
                            model=MODEL, messages=conversation, temperature=0, max_tokens=max_tokens,
                            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
                            extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": think}})
                    reply = await asyncio.wait_for(request,
                        WARM_TIMEOUT if _warm["done"] and not think else CALL_TIMEOUT)
                    _warm["done"] = True
                finally:
                    spent = time.monotonic() - started
                    STATS["seconds"] += spent
                    kind = BY_LABEL.setdefault(label.split(":")[0] if label.startswith("extract") else (label or "call"), [0, 0.0])
                    kind[0] += 1
                    kind[1] += spent
            _count(reply.usage, provider)
            choice = reply.choices[0]
            content = choice.message.content or ""
            parsed = parse_json_object(content)
            if parsed is not None:
                return parsed
            if choice.finish_reason == "length":
                problem = f"the reply was cut off at {max_tokens} tokens"
                if max_tokens >= MAX_TOKENS_CEILING:
                    think = False
                max_tokens = min(max_tokens * 2, MAX_TOKENS_CEILING)
            else:
                problem = f"the reply is not a JSON object: {content[:120]!r}"
                conversation = [*messages, {"role": "assistant", "content": content[:2000]},
                                {"role": "user", "content": REMINDER}]
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            problem = f"no reply within {WARM_TIMEOUT if _warm['done'] and not think else CALL_TIMEOUT} s"
        except APIStatusError as error:
            problem = f"HTTP {error.status_code}: {str(error)[:200]}"
            permanent = error.status_code in PERMANENT
            if error.status_code == 401 and "finished or expired" in str(error).lower():
                _warm["expired"] = True
        except Exception as error:  # the connection, the proxy, a reply without choices
            problem = f"{type(error).__name__}: {str(error)[:200]}"
        STATS["failed"] += 1
        last = attempt == ATTEMPTS or bool(_warm.get("expired")) or (permanent and attempt >= 2)
        print(f"[llm] {label or 'call'}: attempt {attempt} failed, {problem}" + ("; giving up" if last else ""),
              file=sys.stderr)
        if last:
            break
        await asyncio.sleep(min(2 ** attempt, 20) * random.uniform(0.5, 1))
    return {}


def summary() -> str:
    """The run's model use in one line, with what it costs at the hosted model's simulated prices."""
    fresh = STATS["prompt_tokens"] - STATS["cached_tokens"]
    cost = (fresh * PRICE_INPUT + STATS["cached_tokens"] * PRICE_CACHED
            + STATS["completion_tokens"] * PRICE_OUTPUT) / 1_000_000
    return (f"LLM: {STATS['calls']} calls ({STATS['failed']} failed), {STATS['prompt_tokens']} prompt tokens "
            f"({STATS['cached_tokens']} cached), {STATS['completion_tokens']} completion tokens, "
            f"{STATS['seconds']:.0f} s in calls, about ${cost:.4f}; by caller: "
            + ", ".join(f"{name} {calls}x/{seconds:.0f}s" for name, (calls, seconds) in sorted(BY_LABEL.items()))
            + (f"; openai tokens {STATS['openai_tokens']}" if STATS.get("openai_tokens") else ""))

    first request; the backup takes its own. Raises asyncio.TimeoutError when nothing came back within `cap`

"""A model call that gets no reply is given up early and asked a second time, against a fake client (no network)."""
import asyncio
import sys
import unittest
from pathlib import Path
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import patch

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

import llm  # noqa: E402

ANSWER = '{"thought": "ok", "actions": []}'


def reply(content: str = ANSWER) -> SimpleNamespace:
    return SimpleNamespace(usage=SimpleNamespace(prompt_tokens=10, completion_tokens=5, prompt_tokens_details=None),
                           choices=[SimpleNamespace(finish_reason="stop", message=SimpleNamespace(content=content))])


class Completions:
    """Answers each request as scripted: "ok", "hang" (never answers), "slow" (answers after 0.15 s) or "error"."""

    def __init__(self, *script: str):
        self.script, self.sent, self.cancelled = list(script), 0, 0

    async def create(self, **kwargs):
        self.sent += 1
        how = self.script.pop(0) if self.script else "ok"
        try:
            if how == "hang":
                await asyncio.Event().wait()
            if how == "slow":
                await asyncio.sleep(0.15)
            if how == "error":
                raise RuntimeError("connection reset")
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            self.cancelled += 1
            raise
        return reply()


class Backups(unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.saved = dict(llm.STATS)
        for key in llm.STATS:
            llm.STATS[key] = 0
        llm._backups["flying"] = 0
        self.warm = dict(llm._warm)
        llm._warm.clear()
        llm._warm["done"] = True

    def tearDown(self):
        llm.STATS.update(self.saved)
        llm._warm.clear()
        llm._warm.update(self.warm)

    async def ask(self, completions: Completions, cap: float = 0.4, backup_after: float = 0.05, **more):
        client = SimpleNamespace(chat=SimpleNamespace(completions=completions))
        with patch.object(llm, "_session", return_value=(client, asyncio.Semaphore(4))), \
             patch.object(llm, "STEP_CAP", cap), patch.object(llm, "STEP_HEDGE", backup_after), \
             patch.object(llm, "LONG_CAP", cap), patch.object(llm, "LONG_HEDGE", backup_after), \
             patch.object(llm, "RETRY_PAUSE", (0.0, 0.0)):
            return await llm.chat_json([{"role": "user", "content": "next step"}], think=False, label="erp", **more)

    async def test_a_quick_answer_needs_one_request(self):
        completions = Completions("ok")
        self.assertEqual(await self.ask(completions), {"thought": "ok", "actions": []})
        self.assertEqual((completions.sent, llm.STATS["backups"], llm.STATS["failed"]), (1, 0, 0))

    async def test_a_lost_request_is_answered_by_its_backup_and_dropped(self):
        completions = Completions("hang", "ok")
        started = asyncio.get_running_loop().time()
        self.assertEqual(await self.ask(completions), {"thought": "ok", "actions": []})

1	# Deterministic control shells make runs repeatable
2	
3	The spread from 10 to 100 on identical code is a timing and control problem, not a model-capability problem, and the evidence says to fix it with deterministic structure around the model, not with more prompting, more agents or more reasoning. Three of the seven recorded runs reached 100, so Qwen3.8-Flash-Next without thinking can do the task; what changed between runs was which calls hung, which facts arrived first, and whether an agent entered a loop that the harness only warned about. Five remedies carry the weight, in descending order of evidence: bound each model call at 20 to 30 seconds and send one backup request after about 8 seconds, where the code now waits 120 to 150; stop replaying the agent's own thoughts, refuse repeated no-effect actions, and restart a stalled agent in a clean context seeded from a code-built ledger; stamp every question and conclusion with the input values it rests on, so that a correction reopens it, wakes its owner and is announced as a change; gate "absent" and "done" on a harness-recorded coverage ledger with exactly one forced re-check; and hold a signable bid at all times behind a protected submission reserve. Published ablations credit structural changes of this kind with 15.6 points on one multi-agent system and 31% of performance on another, against 5 to 9 points for prompt rewording, and a benchmark shows models repeating a failed action unaware in 23% to 59% of cases even with the repetition visible in context. An LLM orchestrator, a planner call per step, tree search, voting on navigation, LLM-written history summaries, extra trap warnings and thinking mode for navigation are each unsupported for small models, too slow for a 20-minute window, or measured to hurt. Every recommended change leaves navigation, searches and document choice to the model and keys only on structure (page fingerprints, fact kinds, input hashes), so it carries over to websites with other names, layouts and information splits. None has been measured on this stack, so the report grades each claim and ends with a build order and a fault-injection test that proves the mechanisms faster than scored runs can.
4	
5	## Three runs at 100 prove capability; timing and control decide the rest
6	
7	The team's record, as given in the research brief, is three runs at 100 and four between 10 and 45 from one code version. That distribution is bimodal, which points to run-level events (a site lost to a loop, a fact that landed after the cut-off, a hung call that ate two minutes) and not to gradual quality loss. The largest published failure study of multi-agent LLM systems reaches the same reading: across more than 1,600 annotated traces from seven frameworks, **system-design issues account for 44.2% of failures, with step repetition the single largest mode at 15.7%**, followed by reasoning-action mismatch at 13.2% and unawareness of termination conditions at 12.4% ([MAST](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)). The same study measured what repairs buy: refined prompts moved one system from 25.0 to 34.4 and another by about 5 points, while a topology change with an objective check reached 40.6, and its authors conclude that structural changes beat prompt changes without resolving every mode ([MAST](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)). Magentic-One's ablation agrees from the other side: removing its ledgers, progress tracking and loop detection costs **31% of performance** on GAIA validation ([Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468)).
8	
9	The determinism lever is already spent. `starter-kit/llm.py` runs every Qwen call at temperature 0, and the literature says that neither removes variance nor cures navigation failures: at temperature 0 with a fixed seed, accuracy across ten repeats still varied by up to 15% on hosted models ([Atil et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5)), and the same agent on identical inputs produced 2.3 to 4.2 distinct action sequences in ten runs, with consistent tasks reaching 82-87% accuracy and inconsistent ones 41-65% ([Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)). Greedy decoding has a second cost: the original ReAct error analysis suspected it as the reason a model regenerates its previous thought and action and cannot leave the loop ([ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)). A near-identical prompt yields an identical turn, so a loop at temperature 0 is stable, and a warning string that is itself identical every turn becomes part of the repeated pattern.
10	
11	Fan-out arithmetic explains why hangs reach almost every run. A component that is slow once in 100 requests makes a 100-way fan-out slow 63% of the time ([The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)); by the same arithmetic a run of 200 to 260 model calls with a 1% hang rate contains at least one hang in about 93% of runs, and each hang currently costs one agent up to 120 to 150 seconds. The table maps the five observed failure causes to the remedy the evidence supports best. "Strong" means a direct ablation or several independent systems with a mechanism that matches the failure; "moderate" means a measured mechanism whose application here is inferred; "weak" means a design inference with no measurement.
12	
13	| Failure in the bad runs | Best-supported remedy | Nature of the evidence | Strength |
14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| Model calls that hang | Per-attempt cap from logged latency, one backup request at the rolling p90, loser cancelled, start-up canary | Classic tail-latency practice; one simulation and engineering posts for LLM calls; no peer-reviewed LLM study | Strong for the cap, moderate for the backup request |
16	| Agents that loop or repeat | No replay of own thoughts; refusal of repeated no-effect actions keyed on page state; stall counter; clean restart from a code-built ledger | Ablations on history and action space; loop benchmarks on Qwen-family models; ledger ablation; source code of four production detectors | Strong that warnings are insufficient and structure helps; moderate for the exact ladder |
17	| Acting on facts since corrected | Input-basis stamp on every question and conclusion; level-triggered wake; explicit CHANGED line; old thoughts dropped on change | A belief-update benchmark; classic truth maintenance; no measurement of push versus re-reading in LLM teams | Moderate |
18	| Facts that arrive late | Blocked, tentative and ready states; superset filing on the stable attribute; survey budget then hold; bid recomputed on every new record | Prerequisite gating in planner-compiler systems; nothing published on gating by input stability | Weak to moderate |
19	| Searches that cover too little | Harness-written coverage ledger with unopened scopes; one check-again gate on "absent" and "done"; outline in place of truncation | Early-termination findings on three benchmarks; a single re-check measured; the ledger itself unmeasured | Moderate |
20	
21	## A short cap and one backup request erase the two-minute hang penalty
22	
23	The current client waits `WARM_TIMEOUT = 120` seconds for a navigation call and `CALL_TIMEOUT = 150` for an extraction call, then retries in sequence up to five times with backoff; `ask_clef` in `starter-kit/models.py` waits 120 seconds with no retry. Tail-latency practice says this is the wrong shape for a deadline. A hedged request goes out only after the first has been outstanding longer than the 95th-percentile latency and the first answer wins, which limits extra load to about 5% ([The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)). Google's overload rules cap a request at three attempts, hold retries under 10% of a client's requests, and retry at one layer only; without that budget worst-case load grows about threefold, with it about 1.1-fold ([Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)). The difference for a slow model call is structural: sequential retry delivers primary plus retry, hedging delivers the faster of the two ([Tian Pan](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)). In a 50,000-request simulation with 5% stragglers, **hedging at the observed p90 cut p99 latency by about 74% for 8.9% extra requests**, and the same article warns that for streaming endpoints the timer must run on the first token, and that hedging behind a shared rate limit can itself trigger throttling ([InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)). No peer-reviewed study measures hedging of LLM API calls; this evidence is classic systems work plus engineering posts.
24	
25	The team's own numbers make the case sharper than the literature does. Navigation calls run at a median of 3 seconds and a 95th percentile of 9, and in one bad run 9 of roughly 148 attempts never answered. The research team's own lognormal fit to those two percentiles (a calculation, not a published result) puts the 99th percentile near 14 seconds and the share of healthy calls above 30 seconds at 0.03%, so a call silent at 30 seconds is hung, not slow. Their Monte Carlo of one agent's 65 sequential calls at a 6% hang rate gives a median model wait of about 780 seconds under the current policy, 363 with a 30-second cap, 325 with a 20-second cap and 266 to 277 with one backup request sent after 7 to 9 seconds, for 5% extra calls on a healthy day and up to 22% on a bad one. Almost all of the gain comes from the cap; the backup adds the rest and, unlike a very short cap, never discards a primary that is slow but alive.
26	
27	That last property matters because the code records why the timeouts are long: a model scaled to zero answers its first call slowly, a 75-second timeout once cut off a legitimate first turn with a large prompt under load, and extraction calls with thinking on take longer than navigation calls. The change therefore has four parts. Send one backup after the rolling p90 of that call type (start at 8 seconds for thinking-off steps), keep the primary running, take whichever answers first and cancel the other. Set the per-attempt cap per caller label from logged latency, starting at 30 seconds for navigation steps and at the logged 99th percentile for thinking-on extraction, and cut attempts from five to three. Run three parallel one-token calls at start-up as a canary and warm-up, and list every model the agent relies on in `agent.json` so the platform waits for it. Apply the same bounds to Clef. One governor should own concurrency: a semaphore below the shared limit of 32, agent steps ahead of the extraction fan-out, and at most four slots for backups. `MAX_CONCURRENT` is 16 today because test runs may overlap; during the final evaluation no second run of the team should be active, since hedging helps with independent hangs and makes self-inflicted queueing worse. Two facts remain unknown and each takes ten minutes to test: whether a client-side cancel frees the proxy's concurrency slot, and whether the proxy streams, which would let a "no first token" timer separate hung calls from long answers.
28	
29	### The signature is the one step that must never be late

The package on my branch scored **100 twice**: once in 8:55, the team's fastest so far, and again in 12:19 while three other runs were in flight. A third run was lost to a platform failure by the platform's own verdict, so it does not count.

## One thing you need to know first

The first of those test runs now appears as a scored submission (`sub_0af454da`, review passed). I did not submit it. `TEAM.md` records an earlier case where the organisers promoted a test run after an outage, so that is the likely explanation. As your latest passed submission, this is now the package that goes into the final run, and its code is not in git. It exists as uncommitted changes in a temporary working copy, plus a patch file I saved under `research_notes/Reliable multi site web agents/patches/`.

## What is in that package

It is Maria's branch (`288c88c`: loop fixes, the question routing from your v1, browser failover) plus three changes of mine:

- **Bounded model calls with a backup request.** A call with no reply is given up after 30 seconds (75 for extraction) instead of 120 to 150, and a second identical request goes out once the first is unusually slow. The team's tally says model overload decided 13 of 29 runs.
- **Changed-fact notice.** When a requirement value changes after agents have seen it, every agent is told, the open question keeps saying it, and an "absent" given for the old value is reopened.
- **Language note.** Pages can be German or English; search with the site's own words and never translate identifiers.

In the two runs no model call failed. Backup requests were sent 5 and 17 times and answered first 1 and 2 times. The changed-fact notice never had occasion to fire. Maria's loop handling visibly acted in the second run. Two runs cannot tell which change earned the result, and the report estimates about 30 runs to separate 80 % from 95 % reliability.

## Run `44a626ef` and the research

- **The fast 100** was your own v1 package. It was fast because each agent only saw questions its own site can answer, so all four finished by themselves and the investigation ended at 5:21. That routing is keyed on the site names "erp" and "mail", which the final run will not have.
- **The research report is delivered:** [Reliable multi site web agents.md](reports/Reliable multi site web agents.md). Its conclusion is that the spread between runs is a timing and control problem, best fixed with deterministic structure around the model rather than more prompting, more agents or more reasoning. It grades the evidence for five remedies, lists twelve popular ideas not worth doing here, and gives a build order.
- **Applied so far:** the first item of that build order and part of the third. Next would be no longer replaying the agent's own earlier thoughts, then routing that learns which site answers what instead of relying on site names.
